A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same DropoutTS research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–F are readable and support reliable matching despite added experiments and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments on Synth-12 and seven real-world datasets, component ablations, efficiency measurements, and spectral reconstruction analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds generalization experiments, additional datasets and backbones, dropout-rate analysis, and a hard-denoising comparison.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the same detrending, spectral normalization, SFM-guided filtering, residual scoring, adaptive rate mapping, and straight-through dropout procedure. Figure 4 corrects its depiction of trend restoration to match the existing method; no algorithmic revision is established.

E1.justification: Beyond v1’s seven real-world datasets and Synth-12, v2 evaluates financial Exchange Rate and cardiac ECG5000 forecasting in Appendix B.4. Section 5.4 also introduces zero-shot transfer between ETT datasets, adding a distinct distribution-shift scenario.

E2.justification: The original six backbones and Selective Learning comparisons remain. Table 16 adds WPMixer, TimeFilter, and MultiPatchFormer, each evaluated with and without DropoutTS. Table 10 adds a hard-denoising comparator for Informer, PatchTST, and TimeMixer on ILI. SynEVO is discussed but not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: New protocols include PatchTST training on 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of ILI data; eight reported ETT source-target transfers; and a low-pass-filtered input control. Table 17 specifies ECG5000 horizons of 36, 72, 144, and 288. Existing benchmark settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of whether dropout rates reflect sample heterogeneity, robustness to training-data scarcity and distribution shifts, and capacity modulation versus direct denoising. It also expands Selective Learning cost comparisons and revises the detrending reconstruction results in Figure 14. Existing component ablations and sensitivity analyses remain.

E5.justification: The trial visualization in Figure 6 and Pearson correlation analysis in Appendix D.1 remain unchanged. No new seed counts, repeated-run counts, forecasting confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. Table 5 describes variation across sample-level dropout rates, rather than uncertainty in experimental performance.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and ablation tables retain their numerical results, but v2 adds substantial results in Tables 5, 6, 9, 10, 16, and 17. These include exceptions: Table 6 reports worse MSE with DropoutTS at 50% ILI data, 3.143 versus 3.169. Figure 14 replaces Edge-MAE values; under regime shift, OLS changes from 1.38, the worst result, to 0.653, the best. The reason for that numerical revision is not explained.

T1.justification: The signal/noise definitions, method equations, detrending formulation, and Appendix F assumptions, theorems, bound, and proof sketch are unchanged. Updating the Hastie reference does not revise the mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction’s contribution list, and principal conclusion retain the same claims: spectral scoring enables model-agnostic, sample-adaptive capacity modulation with negligible overhead and complementary robustness. The stated 46.0% and 9.8% headline gains remain. Added experiments support these retained contributions.

C2.justification: New interpretations connect dropout-rate dispersion to heterogeneity, few-shot behavior to noise memorization and data redundancy, transfer performance to invariant dynamics, and hard denoising to information loss. The conclusion newly identifies broadly distributed spectral energy as a failure condition. Appendix B.1 also replaces its contradictory description of decreasing error as degradation with a noise-as-regularization interpretation.

D1.justification: Table 9 newly documents Informer+ILI parameter counts and training/pretraining costs, including Selective Learning’s additional 3,000 parameters and 29 seconds of pretraining. The optimizer, hardware, dropout hyperparameters, and code-access statement remain unchanged. Detailed preprocessing and implementation instructions for the added evaluations remain limited.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantive comparison with SynEVO’s model-level adaptation, an Accuracy Law citation supporting its positioning, and a Goldberger et al. citation for the healthcare evaluation. The overall research framing remains. Other year, venue, and authorship corrections concern existing references.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites related-work, experimental, and concluding passages; adds Section 5.4 and Appendix B.4; and introduces limitations, acknowledgements, and a conflict disclosure. Publication and correspondence text also change. The overall narrative organization and most existing exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: Five new tables present dropout distributions, generalization, denoising, newer backbones, and additional domains. The compatibility table expands into accuracy, parameter-cost, and timing blocks. Figure 4 corrects detrending illustrations and labels; Figure 14 adds clean-signal curves and removes highlighted circles, although its caption still mentions them. Most other figures are retained or relocated.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, v2 provides broader empirical scrutiny through transfer, data-scarcity, newer-backbone, and additional-domain evaluations, alongside useful mechanism diagnostics and an explicit applicability limitation. These strengthen the paper, but limited new protocol and uncertainty documentation constrain the gain. Reporting inconsistencies also remain or appear: Table 10 gives identical TimeMixer MAEs of 1.148 while claiming a 0.5% improvement, and Figure 14’s universal-best caption still conflicts with its quadratic-case results.
